usage: First-person pronoun used with close friends, younger people, or family. Plain, not polite.
나 changes to 내 before the subject marker 가. Say 내가, never 나가, for 'I (subject).'
나 + 는. Often shortened to 난 in speech.
나 + 를. Often shortened to 날 in speech.
examples: 나 with the topic marker 는; the 요-ending is still polite even though 나 is casual.
나 becomes 내 before 가, giving 내가 for 'I (subject).'
Can you give this to me?
나 as 'me' in casual everyday speech.
nuance: 나 is the casual word for 'I/me' and is what you use with close friends, people younger than you, and family. It is plain and warm, but using it with elders, strangers, or in formal settings can sound rude — there you switch to the humble 저. Remember the irregular subject form: 나 + 가 becomes 내가, not '나가.'
mistakes: Saying 나가 for 'I (subject)'; the correct form is 내가.
Using 나 with a boss, elder, or stranger — use the humble 저 instead to stay polite.

usage: Second-person pronoun for close friends and people younger than you only.
너 changes to 네 before 가. Many people say it like '니가' to avoid confusion with 내가.
너 + 는. Often shortened to 넌 in speech.
너 + 를. Often shortened to 널 in speech.
examples: 너 with the topic marker 는; used only with close friends.
너 becomes 네 before 가, giving 네가 for 'you (subject).'
nuance: 너 is the casual word for 'you' and is only safe with close friends and people clearly younger than you. With elders, strangers, coworkers, or anyone you respect, Koreans avoid 너 entirely — they use the person's name plus a title, a role word, or simply drop 'you' from the sentence. Note the subject form 네가 is often pronounced like '니가' in real speech, because 네가 and 내가 sound almost identical.
mistakes: Using 너 with an elder, stranger, or boss — it sounds rude; use their name or title instead.
Saying 너가 for 'you (subject)'; the written form is 네가 (commonly pronounced 니가).

usage: Polite, humble first-person pronoun for elders, strangers, and formal situations.
저 changes to 제 before the subject marker 가. Say 제가, never 저가, for 'I (subject).'
저 + 는. The standard polite way to introduce yourself.
examples: 저 + 는 is the standard polite self-introduction.
저 becomes 제 before 가, giving 제가 for 'I (subject).'
nuance: 저 is the humble, polite word for 'I/me' and is the safe default with elders, strangers, customers, and anyone you are not close to. It lowers yourself to show respect, so it pairs naturally with 요-form and formal speech. Like 나, it has an irregular subject form: 저 + 가 becomes 제가, not '저가.' Note this 저 (I) looks the same as 저 meaning 'that over there,' but context makes them clear.
mistakes: Saying 저가 for 'I (subject)'; the correct form is 제가.
Using casual 나 where 저 is expected — with strangers and elders, 저 is the polite choice.

usage: Formal 'you,' but it often sounds cold or confrontational with strangers.
당신 + 이. Used in writing, songs, or between spouses.
당신 + 은. Common in formal writing and ads addressing a reader.
당신 + 을. Often appears in lyrics and literary writing.
examples: You are a really good person.
당신 used warmly, the way spouses or writers address someone.
The food you made is delicious.
당신 + 이 as a subject in a soft, affectionate tone.
당신 between a married couple, a very common romantic use.
nuance: 당신 is a formal word for 'you,' but it is tricky: said to a stranger it can sound cold, distant, or even like you are picking a fight (it shows up in arguments). Its warm, natural homes are between spouses ('dear/honey'), in song lyrics, in poetry, and in formal writing or ads that address 'you, the reader.' In ordinary polite conversation Koreans almost never say 당신 to someone's face — they use a name, a title, or no word for 'you' at all.
mistakes: Using 당신 with a stranger to mean a neutral 'you' — it can sound cold or aggressive; use a name or title.
Assuming 당신 is the polite everyday 'you'; in real speech Koreans usually avoid a direct 'you' word entirely.

usage: The standard, respectful word for one's father.
noun + 예요 after the vowel 지.
The honorific subject marker 께서 replaces 이/가 for elders.
께 is the polite particle used toward elders, instead of 한테/에게.
examples: My father is an office worker.
아버지 as the topic with 는.
honorific 께서 + the honorific verb ending 으세요.
아버지 as the object with 를.
nuance: 아버지 is the standard, respectful word for 'father,' used in polite speech and writing and when speaking about your father to others. The warm, affectionate home word is 아빠, similar to 'dad,' which children and many adults use at home. Because 아버지 is an elder, Koreans often pair it with honorific markers like 께서 and honorific verb endings.
mistakes: Saying 아버지이에요 — after the vowel 지 it must be 아버지예요.
Using casual 아빠 in formal or business settings where 아버지 is expected.

usage: The standard, respectful word for one's mother.
noun + 예요 after the vowel 니.
The honorific subject marker 께서 replaces 이/가 for elders.
께 is the polite particle used toward elders, instead of 한테/에게.
examples: 어머니 as the topic with 는.
honorific 께서 + the honorific verb ending 하세요.
어머니 as the object; 도와드리다 is the humble form of 돕다.
nuance: 어머니 is the standard, respectful word for 'mother,' used in polite speech and writing and when talking about your mother to others. The affectionate home word is 엄마, like 'mom,' which is what people usually call her directly at home. As 어머니 is an elder, it commonly takes honorific markers such as 께서 and honorific verb endings.
mistakes: Saying 어머니이에요 — after the vowel 니 it must be 어머니예요.
Using casual 엄마 in formal settings where the respectful 어머니 is expected.

usage: The bright part of the day, opposite of 밤 (night).
낮 + 에 marks the time when something happens.
낮 + 잠 (sleep) = a daytime sleep, a nap.
낮 paired with 밤 to contrast daytime and nighttime.
examples: 낮 + 에 marks the time of an action.
It is too hot during the day.
낮에는 with the contrast topic marker 는.
I take a nap on weekends.
nuance: 낮 means the daytime, the bright hours between morning and evening, and it stands in contrast to 밤 (night). The final ㅈ links to a following vowel, so 낮에 is pronounced like '나제.' A very common compound is 낮잠 (a nap). Do not confuse 낮 (daytime) with 낯 (face), which sounds similar but is a different, less common word.
mistakes: Confusing 낮 (daytime) with the look-alike 낯 (face) or 낫 (sickle / to be better).
Forgetting the liaison: 낮에 is pronounced '나제,' not 'nat-e.'

usage: Everyday word for color; slightly warmer than the shorter 색.
무슨 + 색깔 asks which color something is.
색깔 + 이 as the subject with an adjective.
the color one likes; 좋아하는 modifies 색깔.
examples: 색깔 as the object with 을 in a question.
This bag has a pretty color.
색깔 as the topic; 파란색 is a specific color.
nuance: 색깔 is the everyday word for 'color' and feels a little fuller and warmer than the short form 색, which often attaches to a specific color name (파란색, 빨간색). You can ask 무슨 색깔이에요? (What color is it?) about almost anything. Both 색깔 and 색 are correct; 색깔 stands alone more naturally, while 색 is the building block inside color names.
mistakes: Trying to attach a color directly to 색깔, like '파란색깔'; specific colors use 색, as in 파란색.
Asking 어떤 색깔 when 무슨 색깔 is the more natural way to ask 'what color.'

usage: The standard color noun for green; 초록 alone is also common.
color + noun, the most common modifier pattern.
a lighter, fresh green; a separate shade word.
I'll take the green one, please
natural way to pick a color at a store.
examples: 색 + 을 좋아해요 states a favorite color.
In spring the leaves are green.
Do you have a green umbrella?
nuance: 초록색 is the standard word for green and covers the typical leaf-and-grass green. In casual speech people often drop 색 and just say 초록, and you may also hear the English loanword 그린 in fashion. A lighter, yellowish spring green is 연두색, a distinct shade, so use 초록색 for ordinary mid-green.
mistakes: Mixing up 초록색 (green) with 연두색 (light yellow-green); they are different shades.
Calling a traffic 'green light' 초록불 is fine, but Koreans very often say 파란불 (blue light) for it by habit.

usage: The standard color noun for white; 하얀색 is an equally common synonym.
color + clothing item, a very common combo.
흰색 + 이에요 to state a color.
I'll take the white one, please
natural way to pick a color at a store.
examples: Which is better, white or black?
nuance: 흰색 is the standard color noun for white and is interchangeable with 하얀색 in most situations; 흰색 sounds a touch more neutral and 하얀색 a touch softer. The matching adjective is 하얗다 (to be white), as in 눈이 하얘요 (the snow is white). For naming the color itself — clothes, cars, paint — 흰색 is a safe, common choice.
mistakes: Confusing the color noun 흰색 with the adjective 하얗다; use 흰색 to name the color, 하얘요 to describe something.
Mixing up 흰색 (white) with 회색 (gray) — they look and sound a bit alike but are different colors.

usage: General word for any alcoholic drink.
술 + 을; alcohol takes 마시다 (drink), not 먹다.
술 + 집 (house) = a place to drink.
literally 'one glass of alcohol'; an invitation to grab a drink.
examples: 술 + 을 with 마시다; 잘 못 = not well / hardly.
Let's have a drink together today.
술 한잔하다 = to grab a drink.
술 with a polite negative command.
nuance: 술 is the general word for any alcoholic drink, covering 소주, 맥주, 막걸리, and more. Like other drinks it takes the verb 마시다 (to drink), not 먹다, though in very casual speech you may hear 술을 먹다 too. Drinking culture is social in Korea: 술 한잔하다 (to have a drink) is a common friendly invitation, and pouring drinks for others is polite.
mistakes: Using 먹다 with 술 in careful speech; the standard verb is 마시다 (술을 마셔요).
Confusing 술 (alcohol) with 물 (water) — one vowel apart but very different drinks.

usage: NATIVE number 하나 → 한 + 시. Hours use native numbers.
NATIVE number 둘 → 두 + 시, not '이 시.'
몇 + 시 asks for the hour: 몇 시예요?
examples: I get up at seven o'clock.
native 일곱 + 시 + 에 marks clock time.
수업이 세 시 삼십 분에 끝나요.
hour 세 시 uses NATIVE 세, but minutes 삼십 분 use SINO numbers.
nuance: 시 is the counter for the o'clock HOUR, and it is one of the trickiest beginner points because the hour uses NATIVE Korean numbers (한 시, 두 시, 세 시, 네 시...), while the MINUTES counter 분 uses SINO-Korean numbers (일 분, 십 분, 삼십 분). So 3:30 is 세 시 삼십 분 — native for the hour, Sino for the minutes. Watch the shape changes before 시: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네. Add 에 to say 'at' a time: 두 시에 (at two o'clock).
mistakes: Using Sino numbers for the hour, like '삼 시' for three o'clock; it must be the native 세 시.
Mixing the systems for minutes — minutes (분) use Sino numbers, so '세십 분' is wrong; say 삼십 분.
